newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Ringgit seen rising to 2.47 by year-end.
newsitem.headline: Ringgit seen rising to 2.47 by year-end.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit remained under pressure from selling by offshore players as well as concern over the Thai baht, but its weakness was seen as temporary, economists said on Tuesday.
Strong economic fundamentals and high interest rates in Malaysia would pull the ringgit out of the slump, they said, expecting the currency to hit 2.47-2.48 per dollar by the end of the year.
The ringgit was quoted at 2.5240/50 a dollar at midday on Tuesday.

Economists said the ringgit has still not overcome the spillover effect of the baht crisis. The Thai currency came under severe attack by speculators in May which prompted intervention by the region's central banks.

"It's still pretty uncertain in Thailand. Baht sentiment is still pretty negative," said Sim Moh Siong, economist with Citibank in Singapore. "But the comparison between Thailand and Malaysia may not be justified."

Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said last month that the impact of the baht crisis would be temporary. The ringgit should not fall much "because the context of the Thai baht is different and the economic fundamentals are different," he said.
"Until we see stability in the baht, there will be a cloud over the regional currencies," said Desmond Supple, head of currency research at BZW in Singapore.

Bank Negara Malaysia intervened last Friday to support the ringgit at 2.5250. Foreign exchange dealers said there was talk that the central bank had placed more orders to sell the dollar at that level.
Economists said that by intervening, the central bank had reaffirmed its preference for a strong ringgit.
The ringgit was unlikely to weaken above 2.5300, they said.
The currency hit a 17-month high of 2.4680 on January 13, this year after ending 1996 at 2.5305.
Economists said the ringgit was currently undervalued and did not reflect the country's economic fundamentals.
"The economy is still among the strongest in the region and barring any fallout from the baht, the ringgit should trade below the 2.50 level," Supple said.
"We are looking at 2.47 by year-end," he said.

The Malaysian Institute of Economic Research, a government-backed think-tank, on Monday maintained its projection of Malaysia's real gross domestic product (GDP) growth at 8.2 percent in 1997 and 8.5 percent in 1998. GDP growth in 1996 was 8.2 percent.
Economists said the interest rate differential would also favour the ringgit.
Though local interbank rates have fallen from their highs in May, they were still much higher than those in neighbouring Singapore.
The benchmark three-month Kuala Lumpur interbank offered rate stood at 7.50 percent on Tuesday, about four percentage points higher than in Singapore.
Some money market dealers said rates were being kept high by Bank Negara to ward off speculators because it would be expensive to maintain short ringgit positions.

"Interest rates in Malaysia have limited scope to come down because of the strong economy. And this should favour the ringgit," said Sim of Citibank. He expects the ringgit to trade at 2.48 a dollar by the end of the year.
